record.paper_title: A survey of open questions in adaptive therapy: bridging mathematics and clinical translation
record.original_question: How should adaptive cancer therapy models incorporate tissue homeostasis, normal cells, stromal cells, vasculature, immune cells, extracellular matrices, and environmentally mediated drug resistance when designing protocols to control cancer? Because cancer cells live in tissue ecosystems and may use stromal refuges that allow sensitive or resistant cells to survive therapy, should models evaluate how to manage or exploit environmentally mediated drug resistance, recapitulate the homeostasis disrupted by carcinogenesis, and design therapy-induced homeostasis rather than modeling only sensitive and resistant cancer cell populations?

evidence.quote: 1.4 What is the role of homeostasis and normal tissue in adaptive therapy?

In reality, the fitness of a cancer cell is not simply a cell-intrinsic property but includes its ability to take advantage of its dynamic tumor environment that includes not just other cancer cells but normal cells, vasculature, immune cells and extra-cellular matrices (see figure 2).

This environmentally mediated drug resistance (EMDR) explains why anti-cancer treatments prove less effective than otherwise expected. In the context of adaptive therapy, EMDR may provide the cancer cells with a therapy refuge regardless of whether they are resistant or sensitive to treatment.

Future adaptive therapy models should allow for EMDR. Such models could more faithfully incorporate the tumor microenvironment and the role of normal cells. Such models could then evaluate how best to manage or exploit EMDR when designing adaptive therapy protocols [55].
Hence, in improving the original adaptive therapy algorithm, we should consider the homeostasis that was disrupted by the tumor as well as the homeostasis that might be engineered by therapy.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a mathematical model of a solid tumor as an ecological system situated within a host tissue. Beyond the usual two-compartment description consisting of drug-sensitive cancer cells $S(t)$ and drug-resistant cancer cells $R(t)$ evolving under a time-dependent treatment schedule $u(t) \in [0,u_{\max}]$, augment the state space to include populations representing:

(i) normal parenchymal cells $N(t)$,
(ii) stromal cells $F(t)$ (e.g., fibroblasts),
(iii) a vasculature compartment $V(t)$ describing local nutrient/oxygen delivery,
(iv) immune effector cells $I(t)$,
(v) an extracellular matrix density $E(t)$, and
(vi) a mechanism of environmentally mediated drug resistance (EMDR), whereby contact with stromal niches, ECM components, or hypoxic regions of vasculature confers transient protection from treatment to both sensitive and resistant cancer cells.

Tissue homeostasis is encoded as a stable steady state of $(N,F,V,I,E)$ in the absence of cancer cells, and carcinogenesis is modeled as a perturbation that destabilizes this state.

Formulate a coupled dynamical system (e.g., ODE, PDE, or stochastic agent-based model) of the variables above with explicit terms for EMDR-mediated transient protection, and pose the following control problem:

Find an adaptive treatment schedule $u(\cdot)$, possibly using only clinically observable feedback such as total tumor burden, that
(a) prevents competitive release of the resistant population $R(t)$ over a long time horizon $T$,
(b) exploits or manages EMDR refuges rather than being defeated by them, and
(c) drives the host tissue compartments $(N,F,V,I,E)$ toward a therapy-induced homeostatic equilibrium that approximates the pre-cancer steady state.

Specifically: identify model structures and feedback control laws for $u(t)$ for which such therapy-induced homeostasis is achievable, characterize necessary conditions on the EMDR mechanism under which long-term tumor control is feasible, and quantify the improvement in time-to-progression compared with adaptive schedules that ignore the microenvironment.
artifact.status_search_result: This is an open research direction in mathematical oncology. While individual aspects—such as incorporating stromal niches, immune compartments, or EMDR into tumor-microenvironment models—have been explored in scattered works, no comprehensive framework integrating tissue homeostasis, normal/stromal/immune/ECM/vasculature components, and EMDR into adaptive therapy protocol design has been established. Recent literature (2023–2025) continues to call for such models, indicating the problem remains open.

status_evidence.title: Mathematical models of the tumor microenvironment and adaptive therapy (recent reviews)
status_evidence.snippet: Ongoing studies continue to extend adaptive therapy models to include stromal/immune compartments and EMDR, without a consensus framework.
status_evidence.claim: No comprehensive resolved framework exists in the recent literature.
